text: Carl Van Vechten (/væn ˈvɛktən/; June 17, 1880 – December 21, 1964) was an American writer and artistic photographer who served as a patron of the Harlem Renaissance and the literary executor of Gertrude Stein. He gained fame as a writer and notoriety for his 1926 novel *Nigger Heaven*. Born in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, he was the youngest child of Charles Duane Van Vechten and Ada Amanda Van Vechten (née Fitch), both of whom were well educated; his father was a wealthy banker and his mother established the Cedar Rapids Public Library and had strong musical talent. Van Vechten developed a passion for music and theatre as a child and graduated from Washington High School in 1898. In 1899, he enrolled at the University of Chicago, where he studied music, art, and opera and began writing for the *University of Chicago Weekly*. After graduating in 1903, he worked as a columnist for the *Chicago American* under the name "The Chaperone," covering topics through semi-autobiographical gossip and criticism, which marked his first experimentation with photography. He was later fired due to his elaborate writing style, which some described as "lowering the tone" of the Hearst papers. In 1906, he moved to New York City and became the assistant music critic at *The New York Times*, where he took a leave in 1907 to travel to Europe to explore opera. In England, he married Anna Snyder, a longtime friend from Cedar Rapids, and returned to *The New York Times* in 1909, becoming the first American critic of modern dance. Through mentorship from Mabel Dodge Luhan, he became immersed in the avant-garde, attending premieres by Isadora Duncan, Anna Pavlova, and Loie Fuller in New York and Paris, where he met Gertrude Stein in 1913. He became a devoted friend and champion of Stein, corresponding with her for the rest of her life and appointing Van Vechten as her literary executor after her death, helping to publish her unpublished works. In a 1915 article titled "How to Read Gertrude Stein," Van Vechten argued that Stein's works require an "expert insider" and that "special writers require special readers." His marriage to Snyder ended in 1912, and he married actress Fania Marinoff in 1914. They were known for defying racial separation by inviting Black people to their home and attending Black social events. Although their marriage lasted 50 years, they frequently argued over Van Vechten’s affairs with men. He maintained a circle of young men, including Donald Angus, Jimmie Daniels, Max Ewing, and Prentiss Taylor, and had romantic and sexual relationships with men, especially Mark Lutz (1901–1968), whom he met in 1931 through Hunter Stagg. Lutz was a model for Van Vechten’s early photography experiments and remained a close friend until Van Vechten’s death; at Lutz’s death, his 10,000 letters to Van Vechten were destroyed as per his wishes, and he donated Van Vechten’s photographs to the Philadelphia Museum of Art. Between 1915 and 1920, several books of Van Vechten’s essays on music and literature were published, and he served as an informal scout for Alfred A. Knopf, who published seven of his novels between 1922 and 1930, beginning with *Peter Whiffle: His Life and Works* and ending with *Parties*. His homoerotic portraits of working-class men reflect his sexuality. As an art appreciator, Van Vechten was drawn to the creativity and racial tolerance of Harlem, where he felt most accepted as a gay man and promoted major figures of the Harlem Renaissance, including Paul Robeson, Langston Hughes, Ethel Waters, Richard Wright, Zora Neale Hurston, and Wallace Thurman. His controversial novel *Nigger Heaven* was published in 1926, which he called "my Negro novel," intended to depict African American life in Harlem rather than Southern racial suffering. Despite criticism, including from W. E. B. Du Bois and Wallace Thurman, who dismissed it as "cheap melodrama," the novel received praise from supporters such as Nella Larsen, Langston Hughes, and Gertrude Stein, who defended it for bringing Harlem culture and racial issues to national attention. Du Bois and later Ralph Ellison and David Levering Lewis criticized the novel as a "colossal fraud" and a "bad influence" driven by commercialism and patronizing sympathy. At age 40, Van Vechten published *Peter Whiffle*, which established his reputation as a novelist and is recognized as an important work in Harlem Renaissance history; he also wrote *The Tattooed Countess*, a fictionalized account of his childhood in Cedar Rapids, and *The Tiger in the House*, which explores his beloved cat. His older brother Ralph died on June 28, 1927, and when Ralph’s widow Fannie died in 1928, Van Vechten inherited $1 million from a trust fund, which remained unaffected by the 1929 stock market crash and provided financial support for him and Fania. By 1930, at age 50, he stopped writing and turned to photography, using his apartment at 150 West 55th Street as a studio, where he photographed many notable individuals. He died in 1964 at age 84 in New York City, and his ashes were scattered over the Shakespeare Garden in Central Park. He was the subject of biographies by Bruce Kellner (1968) and Edward White (2014), and portrayed by Oliver Platt in the 2015 HBO film *Bessie*, which features a discussion of *Nigger Heaven*. His personal papers are held by the Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library at Yale University, and the Beinecke Library also holds "Living Portraits: Carl Van Vechten's Color Photographs of African Americans, 1939–1964," a collection of 1,884 color Kodachrome slides. The Library of Congress holds approximately 1,400 photographs acquired in 1966 from Saul Mauriber, the Prentiss Taylor collection at the Smithsonian’s Archives of American Art, and a Van Vechten collection at Fisk University. The Museum of the City of New York holds 2,174 of his photographs, and Brandeis University holds 1,689 portraits. Van Vechten also donated materials to Fisk University to form the George Gershwin Memorial Collection of Music and Musical Literature. The Philadelphia Museum of Art holds one of the largest collections of Van Vechten’s photographs in the United States, beginning with a 1949 gift of sixty photographs and expanded in 1965 by Mark Lutz, who donated over 12,000 photographs, including portraits of Harlem Renaissance figures like Langston Hughes, Ella Fitzgerald, Billie Holiday, Zora Neale Hurston, and Cab Calloway, as well as artists such as Marcel Duchamp, Henri Matisse, Gaston Lachaise, Joan Miró, and Frida Kahlo, and photographs from the 1939 New York World’s Fair and travels in Western Europe and Northern Africa from 1935–1936. In 1980, concerned about the deterioration of his 35 mm nitrate negatives, photographer Richard Benson, with the Eakins Press Foundation, produced 50 handmade gravure prints, resulting in the album *O, Write My Name: American Portraits, Harlem Heroes*, completed in 1983, which was transferred to the Smithsonian American Art Museum’s permanent collection. The National Portrait Gallery in London holds 17 of Van Vechten’s portraits of leading creative figures. Over 3,000 of his portraits, primarily from the Library of Congress, are available on Wikimedia Commons, illustrating numerous Wikipedia entries on mid-century American notables.
